hints: Differentiate f(x)=(x−a)²g(x) with the product rule.
Factor x−a from the complete derivative and explicitly conclude it is a factor.
walkthrough:
Apply the product rule to differentiate $f(x) = (x - a)^2 g(x)$ with respect to $x$:
$$u = (x - a)^2 \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2(x - a)$$
$$v = g(x) \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = g'(x)$$
$$f'(x) = 2(x - a)g(x) + (x - a)^2 g'(x)$$

Factor out the common term $(x - a)$ from both terms:
$$f'(x) = (x - a)\left[2g(x) + (x - a)g'(x)\right]$$

Conclude that $(x - a)$ is a factor of $f'(x)$:
$$\text{Since } f'(x) = (x - a)h(x) \text{ where } h(x) = 2g(x) + (x - a)g'(x) \text{ is a polynomial,}$$
$$(x - a) \text{ is a factor of } f'(x) \quad (\text{or equivalently } f'(a) = 0).$$

ai_rubric.Differentiation: The product rule gives $f'(x)=(x-a)^2g'(x)+2(x-a)g(x)=(x-a)[(x-a)g'(x)+2g(x)]$, so $x-a$ is a factor.

hints: A repeated factor (x−3)² gives f(3)=0 and f′(3)=0.
Substitute into f(x)=2x³−4x²+px+q, solve the two linear conditions, and verify both.
walkthrough:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - 4x^2 + px + q$. Since $(x - 3)^2$ is a factor of $f(x)$, with $a = 3$:
$$f(3) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f'(3) = 0$$

Differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:
$$f'(x) = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(2x^3 - 4x^2 + px + q\right) = 6x^2 - 8x + p$$

State the values of $p$ and $q$:
$$p = -30, \quad q = 72$$
